name: Probability
seoDesc: Probability: work out probability from the probability. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The probability calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports probability immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Probability calculator work?
sections.html:
The Probability calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports probability in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of probability and the event to test); then you type in the probability (Probabilities for a series of events).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Probability calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

P(A∩B)=probability of A: P(A) × probability of B: P(B)
P(A∪B)=-probability of A: P(A) × probability of B: P(B) + probability of A: P(A) + probability of B: P(B)
Probability of B: P(B)=(probability of A: P(A) − P(A∆B)) ÷ (2 × probability of A: P(A) − 1)
Probability of B: P(B)=(probability of A: P(A) + P((A∪B)') − 1) ÷ (probability of A: P(A) − 1)
Probability of A: P(A)=1 − P(A')
Probability of B: P(B)=1 − P(B')

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Probability of A: P(A) = 10 %, Probability of B: P(B) = 10 %, Type of probability set to A and B both occurring and Event to test set to A always occurring. Working through the relationship above gives P(A∩B) = 1 %, P(A∪B) = 19 %, P(A∆B) = 18 % and P((A∪B)') = 81 %.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: P(A∩B) = 1 %, P(A∪B) = 19 %, P(A∆B) = 18 % and P((A∪B)') = 81 % should be roughly the size you expected from Probability of A: P(A) = 10 % and Probability of B: P(B) = 10 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Probability calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the probability — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Probability calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns probability, derived from the probability. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Probability calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the probability, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter probability of A: P(A) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Probability of A: P(A) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports P(A∩B) = 1 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Probability calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
